name: THE GROOVE IS IN THE CHARD BURGER

recipe.history:
Swiss chard — Beta vulgaris subsp. cicla — despite its name, is not Swiss at all. The plant originated in the Mediterranean basin, with its earliest cultivation traced to Sicily and the coastal regions of North Africa and the Middle East, where wild forms of the beet family grew along rocky shores thousands of years ago. The Moors brought cultivated chard across North Africa and into the Iberian Peninsula during their centuries of Andalusian influence, and from there it spread throughout Mediterranean Europe. The 'Swiss' designation is something of a botanical misnomer, attached to the plant in the nineteenth century by a Swiss botanist named Koch who formally described the species — the Swiss had nothing particular to do with growing or eating it. In its many forms — green chard with white ribs, ruby chard with crimson stalks, golden chard, and the gloriously multicolored rainbow chard with its stems in fuchsia, yellow, orange, and white — the plant has been a foundational green of Mediterranean cooking for centuries. Its large, crinkled leaves wilt beautifully under heat and carry a mild earthiness that anchors garlic and olive oil the way few greens can.

Swiss chard arrived in American home gardens and kitchen tables largely through the influence of Italian and Mediterranean immigrant communities in the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries, where it was prized as a cooking green that could be grown easily in poor soil and harvested across a long season. It sat for decades in the shadow of more fashionable greens — spinach got all the marketing, kale got all the Instagram posts in the 2010s — but chard was always there, quietly excellent. Its transition onto burgers came through the gourmet vegetable movement and the farm-to-table revolution of the 2000s and 2010s, when chefs began treating green toppings not as afterthoughts of texture and color but as major flavor components. Sautéed chard with garlic and olive oil, slightly wilted but still holding its toothsome structure, became a natural complement to rich beef patties — its slight bitterness cutting through fat in the same way a well-dressed salad cuts through a heavy meal.

I grew up thinking chard was the green my grandmother used when she had run out of everything else, and I was embarrassingly wrong about that for most of my early life. It took working a summer at a small farm stand, where I was handed a bunch of rainbow chard at six in the morning and told to just eat a raw leaf, to understand what the fuss was about. Raw, it tasted bright and slightly metallic and green in the most elemental way. Wilted in a cast-iron pan with four smashed garlic cloves and a generous pour of olive oil, with a pinch of crushed red pepper and a squeeze of lemon at the end, it transformed into something I could have eaten straight from the pan with a spoon and a complete lack of shame. I did eat it straight from the pan. I had no shame.

A burger cooked to medium rare — that steadfast 130 to 135 degrees Fahrenheit internal temperature — has a specific relationship with leafy green toppings that well-done burgers simply cannot replicate. The residual warmth of a properly rested medium-rare patty is just enough to gently warm the sautéed chard laid over it, keeping it soft without causing it to steam and turn gray. The pink juices from the patty flow down through the layers of chard, picking up garlic and olive oil on the way to the bottom bun, turning the bread into something extraordinary. Overcook the patty and those juices are gone. Overcook the patty and the chard sits atop a dry gray disc with no moisture to mingle with, no fat to flow, no reason at all to be there. Medium rare is the only temperature that treats every element of this burger — the beef, the chard, the bread — with the generosity they deserve.
ingredients: 3 cups all-purpose flour, plus more for dusting
1/2 cup mashed russet potato (about 1 medium potato, boiled and riced)
2 large eggs (1 for dough, 1 for egg wash)
2 large bunches rainbow chard (about 1 1/2 lbs), stems and leaves separated
Kosher salt and white pepper to taste
1/2 small red onion, very thinly sliced and soaked in cold water 10 minutes
Extra virgin olive oil for finishing
instructions: 1. ROAST THE GARLIC FOR AIOLI: Wrap 6 unpeeled garlic cloves in foil with a drizzle of olive oil. Roast at 400°F (205°C) for 35 to 40 minutes until completely soft and golden. Squeeze cloves from skins and set aside.
2. MAKE THE POTATO ROLLS — DAY BEFORE: Combine yeast, warm water, and 1 teaspoon of the sugar in the bowl of a stand mixer. Let stand 5 minutes until foamy.
3. Add mashed potato, warm milk, remaining sugar, salt, 1 egg, and butter. Add both flours and mix on low with the dough hook until combined, about 2 minutes.
4. Increase to medium and knead 8 to 10 minutes until a smooth, slightly tacky dough forms. The potato makes this dough softer than standard brioche — resist adding too much extra flour.
5. Transfer to an oiled bowl, cover with plastic wrap, and refrigerate overnight.

6. Next day, punch down dough and divide into 6 equal portions. Shape into smooth round balls. Place on parchment-lined baking sheet. Proof at room temperature, covered, 2 to 2 1/2 hours until puffed.
7. Preheat oven to 375°F (190°C). Brush with egg wash. Bake 15 to 17 minutes until golden brown. Cool on a wire rack.

8. MAKE THE GARLIC-LEMON AIOLI: Mash 4 roasted garlic cloves to a smooth paste. Whisk with egg yolks and mustard. Stream in neutral oil very slowly while whisking to form a thick emulsion. Stream in olive oil. Whisk in lemon juice and zest. Season with salt and white pepper. Refrigerate until needed.

9. SAUTÉ THE CHARD: Cut chard stems into 1/2-inch pieces and slice the leaves into 2-inch ribbons, keeping them separate. Heat olive oil in a wide skillet over medium heat. Add garlic and red pepper flakes and cook 1 to 2 minutes until fragrant but not browned.
10. Add chard stems. Cook 3 to 4 minutes until softened. Add chard leaves in batches, tossing with tongs as each batch wilts down to make room for the next. Season with salt and pepper.

11. Cook 4 to 5 minutes until leaves are fully wilted and tender but still bright in color. Remove from heat. Squeeze lemon juice over the top, add lemon zest, toss to coat. Taste and adjust seasoning. Set aside.

12. FORM THE PATTIES: Gently combine ground chuck and ground sirloin. Season with salt, pepper, and smoked paprika. Form into 6 patties, 4 1/2 inches wide and 3/4 inch thick, with a center dimple. Refrigerate 20 minutes.
13. COOK THE PATTIES: Heat a cast-iron skillet over high heat until smoking. Add a thin film of neutral oil. Cook patties without pressing, 3 minutes on the first side until deeply browned.

14. Flip once. Lay a slice of Gruyère over each patty. Cook 2 to 2 1/2 minutes more. Check internal temperature — target 130 to 135°F (54 to 57°C) for medium rare. The Gruyère should be melted and beginning to bubble. Transfer to a wire rack and rest 3 minutes.
15. TOAST THE ROLLS: Split rolls and toast cut-side down in a hot dry skillet 60 to 90 seconds until golden.
16. ASSEMBLE: Spread garlic-lemon aioli on both cut sides of each roll. Place a mound of sautéed chard on the bottom bun. Set the cheese-covered patty on top of the chard.
17. Add drained red onion slices. Drizzle lightly with extra virgin olive oil and finish with a pinch of flaky sea salt. Close with the top bun and serve immediately.
